titleEn: Incline Your ear, LORD, and answer me
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | Bb A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Seventeen verses, the only psalm attributed to David in the third book of the Psalter, and a clean place to see how biblical Hebrew builds a plea: almost every line is an imperative followed by a reason clause opening with ki, for. Verse 8 is the sentence with which the Torah is taken from the ark on Shabbat, and verse 15 repeats the formula of the Thirteen Attributes from Exodus 34:6. Watch the divine names as you read: the title Adonai falls seven times, the four letter name four times, and the psalm changes register around them.

stichs.en: A prayer of David.
Incline Your ear, LORD, answer me,
for I am poor and needy.

verses.summary: The psalm names itself a prayer and names its speaker poor in the same breath. The request is grounded on need, not on standing, and every later ground is measured against this one.

stichs.en: Guard my soul, for I am devoted;
save Your servant, You who are my God,
the one who trusts in You.

verses.summary: The ground shifts from need to loyalty, then off the speaker entirely: the last clause makes trust, not merit, the reason. Three arguments are stacked in a single verse.

stichs.en: Be gracious to me, my Lord,
for to You I call all the day.

verses.summary: Persistence is offered as evidence. Not that the speaker deserves an answer, but that he has not stopped asking, and the asking fills the whole day.

stichs.en: Gladden the soul of Your servant,
for to You, my Lord, I lift up my soul.

verses.summary: The same noun, soul, is the object of both halves: God is asked to gladden what the speaker is already handing over. Lifting the soul is a posture of release, not of grasping.

stichs.en: For You, my Lord, are good and forgiving,
and abundant in kindness to all who call You.

verses.summary: The first verse that asks for nothing. It states what God is, so that the requests around it have something to rest on other than the speaker.

stichs.en: Give ear, LORD, to my prayer,
and attend to the voice of my pleas.

verses.summary: Two imperatives of hearing in parallel, and nothing else asked for. The whole verse requests attention rather than rescue.

stichs.en: In the day of my trouble I call You,
for You will answer me.

verses.summary: The reason clause here is not a claim about the speaker at all. It states the outcome in the imperfect, as something that will happen, and the calling follows from that.

stichs.en: There is none like You among the gods, my Lord,
and there is nothing like Your works.

verses.summary: The lament stops for three verses of praise, and this is the opening of them. Whether the comparison is with other gods or with lesser divine beings is disputed; the Hebrew says only that there is nothing in that class resembling God.

stichs.en: All the nations that You made
will come and bow low before You, my Lord,
and give honor to Your name.

verses.summary: The frame widens from one poor man to every nation, and the reason they come is that God made them. It is the same argument the speaker has been making about himself, scaled up.

stichs.en: For You are great and do wonders;
You are God, You alone.

verses.summary: The praise section compresses to two words at the end: God, alone. Everything the nations of verse 9 will come to acknowledge is stated here as already true.

stichs.en: Teach me, LORD, Your way;
I will walk in Your truth.
Make my heart one, to fear Your name.

verses.summary: The one request in the psalm that is not for rescue. A divided heart is treated as the ordinary condition, and singleness of heart as something that has to be given.

stichs.en: I will thank You, my Lord my God, with all my heart,
and honor Your name forever.

verses.summary: The vow answers the plea of verse 11 in its own vocabulary: whole heart, and the name. What was asked for in one verse is promised back in the next.

stichs.en: For Your kindness toward me is great,
and You have delivered my soul from the lowest Sheol.

verses.summary: A perfect tense in the middle of a plea. Whether it reports a rescue that already happened or states a coming one with the confidence of the past is disputed, and the Hebrew allows both.

stichs.en: God, insolent men have risen against me,
a band of ruthless men have sought my life,
and they have not set You before them.

verses.summary: The lament resumes with no transition. The enemies are defined by an absence: they have not put God in front of them, which is exactly the posture the speaker has held since verse 1.

stichs.en: But You, my Lord, are a God compassionate and gracious,
slow to anger, abundant in kindness and truth.

verses.summary: The reply to verse 14, and it is a quotation: the words of Exodus 34:6, the formula recited as the Thirteen Attributes. Against a company that ignores God, the answer offered is a God defined by patience.

stichs.en: Turn to me and be gracious to me;
give Your strength to Your servant,
and save the son of Your maidservant.

verses.summary: Four imperatives in nine words, the densest asking in the psalm. The speaker identifies himself only by relation, twice: Your servant, and the son of Your maidservant.

stichs.en: Work with me a sign for good,
and let those who hate me see it and be ashamed,
for You, LORD, have helped me and comforted me.

verses.summary: What is asked for is not the fall of the enemies but something visible. The closing verbs are perfect: help and comfort are spoken of as already given, before the sign has been asked for.

pardes.body: The psalm alternates between asking and describing, and the joints are easy to see. Verses 1 to 7 ask, each imperative followed by a clause opening with ki, for. Verses 8 to 10 stop asking and describe God. Verse 11 asks for something new, a whole heart, and verse 12 vows the thanks. Verse 14 returns to the enemies, verse 15 answers them with the attribute formula, and verses 16 and 17 ask again. Read the reason clauses in order and you get the argument by itself: I am poor, I am devoted, I trust, I call all day, You are good, You will answer, Your kindness is great.

Verse 15 is a quotation. Its words are those of Exodus 34:6, and the psalm keeps the sequence compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in kindness and truth, then stops where Exodus continues. The rare word is {{11.5}}, the verb translated here as make one. Its sense is contested: most read a plea for an undivided heart, while others attach it to a root of gladness, which would make the line ask for a glad heart rather than a single one. The page does not settle it. Note also {{16.8}}, son of Your maidservant, which is not a description of birth but a claim of belonging to a household.

The reception of this psalm turned one private verse into a public one. {{8.0}} begins the sentence said when the ark is opened and the Torah taken out on Shabbat and festivals, so a line written by a man who called himself poor and needy is now the congregation's opening move. Read that way, the poor and needy of verse 1 is not only David: the community takes his words as its own without changing them, and the request of verse 11 for one heart is heard as a request for a congregation that wants one thing.

Count the names. The title Adonai appears seven times in this psalm and the four letter name four times, and the two are not scattered at random: the four letter name carries the requests to be heard, in verses 1, 6, 11 and 17, while Adonai carries the descriptions of what God is. In the kabbalistic reading, the plea of {{11.5}} for one heart is the human side of a unity being asked for above, so that the psalm's real request is not rescue from enemies but the removal of division, in the speaker first and then in the nations of verse 9 who come and bow as one.
